The Pompano dolphinfish (Coryphaena equiselis) is a fast-growing pelagic predator found in warm oceanic waters worldwide, closely related to the larger common dolphinfish. Newly hatched larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00017 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00017 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of about 0.69 millimeters. Embryonic development is brief, with the age at birth reaching approximately 3.5 days [ab = approximately 3.5 days] at a water temperature of 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C], a duration comparable to that documented for the closely related common dolphinfish, Coryphaena hippurus. This rapid hatching is typical of small-egged pelagic spawners that produce large numbers of offspring with minimal individual investment.

Juvenile Pompano dolphinfish grow rapidly, reaching the onset of sexual maturity at a total length at puberty of 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 123 grams [Wwp = approximately 123 grams], reflecting the considerable somatic investment achieved within a short developmental window. This swift progression to reproductive size is characteristic of the genus Coryphaena, which is known for one of the fastest growth rates among teleost fishes.

Adults of this species attain an ultimate total length of 146 centimeters [Li = 146 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 34,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 34,600 grams]. This substantial adult body size, achieved within just a few years of hatching, supports the species' role as an active pelagic predator of small fishes and squid in the open ocean. Longevity in the Pompano dolphinfish is short, with a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] at 22.3 °C [T = 22.3 °C]. This compressed lifespan, combined with rapid growth and early maturation at 22 centimeters [Lp = 22 centimeters], reflects a fast-paced life-history strategy typical of small pelagic predators that experience high natural mortality but compensate through rapid population turnover and opportunistic exploitation of productive oceanic frontal zones.
